instructions:
Read the paper below and produce a structured summary.

It matched these tracked topics; `relevance` must contain one entry per slug, stating what this paper changes for that topic:
- overthinking: Overthinking — When and why large reasoning models think more than a problem needs (or less than it needs) — the accuracy/efficiency tradeoff of reasoning length, test-time compute scaling, and methods to make a model stop, or keep going, at the right point.

Rules:
- Write in en.
- Ground every statement in the supplied material. If something is not stated,
  leave the field empty rather than inferring it.
- No marketing language. Prefer the specific number over the adjective.
- Return one JSON object matching the schema exactly. No prose around it.

concepts: string - reusable ideas this paper relies on or introduces
datasets: string - datasets, benchmarks, corpora or simulators used
output_schema.limitations: string - stated limits plus any the reader should notice
output_schema.method: string - how it works, enough for a reader to explain it
methods: string - named methods, architectures or algorithms
output_schema.one_liner: string - what the paper does, in one sentence, no hype
output_schema.problem: string - the problem it addresses and why it is open

relevance.<topic-slug>: string - why this matters for that specific topic

output_schema.results: string - headline numbers, on which benchmarks, against what

payload.title: From Reasoning Traces to Reusable Modules: Understanding Compositional Generalization in Language Model Reasoning

contributions: A hierarchical latent selection model in which reasoning traces come from a cascade of discrete choices over reusable atomic modules, split into skills and routing mechanisms
A theoretical result that SFT and RL are asymmetric and complementary: SFT supplies module material in compound traces, RL decomposes them to identify latent modules
Controlled synthetic benchmark of 24 atomic skills and 10 new atomic routing mechanisms composed to varying depth
Empirical finding that training on compound traces generalises better than training on isolated atomic modules (42.6% vs 14.8% OOD at depth 4)
A data protocol: SFT covers all atomic modules via compositional traces, RL targets compositions outside the SFT support
datasets: synthetic string transformation tasks (24 atomic skills, 10 atomic routing mechanisms)
result.limitations: The authors state the empirical study is deliberately simplified so that compositional structure can be controlled precisely, and name extension to math, code and tool use as future work. The main evidence is therefore synthetic string transformation, not natural reasoning; the real-model component is an analysis of 643 problems with a single 4B model rather than a test of the theory's predictions. Model scale is not varied. The theory identifies conditions under which RL can recover latent modules but the experiments do not establish that this is what happens in production post-training pipelines.
result.method: Reasoning traces are modelled as generated by a cascade of discrete latent selection variables, each picking a reusable atomic module. Modules are of two kinds: skills, which are local operations, and routing mechanisms, which decide how intermediate results are selected, reused and composed. Under this hierarchical latent selection model the authors prove SFT and RL play asymmetric complementary roles -- SFT supplies the raw module material inside compound traces, while RL's exploration gives the coverage needed to identify the latent modules and recombine them. The theory is tested in a controlled synthetic setting: 24 atomic skills taken from prior work plus 10 newly designed atomic routing mechanisms, composed by nesting functions and routing structures to varying depth, which lets the authors manipulate support coverage and composition structure directly. A separate analysis looks at 643 math problems from MATH-500, AIME 2024/2025, AMC and GSM8K with Qwen3-4B.
result.one_liner: Argues that the SFT-then-RL recipe works because RL decomposes compound reasoning traces into reusable atomic modules, formalises this as a hierarchical latent selection model, and tests it on synthetic string-transformation tasks.
result.problem: Post-training combines supervised fine-tuning with reinforcement learning, and the combination reasons better than either alone, but there is no account of why. The paper asks what each stage contributes, and specifically why RL generalises to task combinations never seen in training while SFT tends not to.

relevance.overthinking: Tangential. The paper is about what makes reasoning generalise compositionally and how SFT and RL divide that work; it does not discuss reasoning length, test-time compute scaling, stopping criteria, or the accuracy/efficiency tradeoff at all. It matched on the keyword 'reasoning trace', which here names the object of study rather than a length concern. The one indirect bearing on the topic is that it treats a trace as a composition of discrete modules at some depth -- which makes trace depth a property of the problem's compositional structure rather than a free parameter -- but the paper draws no efficiency conclusion from that, and neither should a reader without further work.

result.results: On the synthetic tasks, RL adds 43.7 points over SFT-only on recovery of individual atomic skills when trained on depth-3 compound traces, and stays ahead across composition depths on unseen compositions by 40.3 points on average. On out-of-distribution compound traces at depth 4, SFT+RL trained on compound traces reaches 42.6% accuracy against 14.8% when RL is run on isolated atomic modules -- i.e. training on compound traces generalises better than training on the atoms themselves. Pairing SFT and RL data over disjoint distributions generalises better than overlapping them, supporting the proposed protocol: SFT covers every atomic module through compositional traces, RL explores compositions outside the SFT support.
